title: Consider the Birds
subtitle: A five-session study on anxiety, and the peace Christ gives instead.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who are tired of being told to stop worrying by people who have never lain awake at three in the morning doing the math on a life that will not balance. It walks slowly through five movements drawn from James Bell's book Consider the Birds, on what anxiety is and is not, on the birds and the lilies Jesus told us to look at, on the peace Paul describes from a prison cell, on casting the weight onto the One who actually cares, and on the rest Christ offers to people who are tired in a way sleep does not touch. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with zero preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This is not a study that tells anxious people their faith would fix them if it were stronger. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. Some anxiety is the soul reaching for the wrong refuge, and the gospel speaks to that with power. Some anxiety is a body that has stopped producing what it needs, a wiring that misfires, a grief that has not finished, and that anxiety needs a doctor and is no more a sin than a broken arm. The study holds both without flinching, and refuses to make the second sound like the first. Most of all it implicates the leader and the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He has lain awake. He has white-knuckled a morning he had no reason to fear and called it discernment. He has preached peace on a Sunday and gripped the wheel all the way home. He writes from inside the worry. So will you.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: What Anxiety Actually Is
sessions.aim: To name anxiety honestly, neither as a sin to be scolded out of people nor as a thing too delicate to touch, and to refuse both the preacher who shames the worried and the lie that a worried Christian is a faithless one.
sessions.summary: A woman told Bell after a service that she had prayed harder than anyone she knew and still could not breathe some mornings, and she wanted to know what she was doing wrong. She was not doing anything wrong. She was carrying something, and somebody had told her the carrying was unbelief. The first question is not how to stop being anxious. It is what anxiety even is. Bell takes the strong form of two answers that want to silence each other. The first says anxiety is a spiritual failure, a small faith, a refusal to trust, and it is right that Jesus does say do not be anxious, right that some of our worry is the heart trusting the wrong thing. The second says anxiety is purely medical, a chemical event, nothing to do with the soul, and it is right that a body can break in ways no prayer reaches, right that shaming a sick person is cruelty dressed as theology. Bell will not let either win cleanly. Anxiety is not always sin, which refutes the scolder, and anxiety is not always only chemistry, which refutes the reductionist. It is sometimes the soul afraid, sometimes the body failing, often both at once, and the pastoral work is to tell which without pretending you always can. Jesus does not open with a rebuke. He says look at the birds. The cure begins not with shame but with attention turned outward, toward a God who feeds what cannot sow.

keyScripture.why: Jesus begins not with a command to feel differently but with therefore do not be anxious about your life, naming worry as a thing that fastens onto the basics of survival, food and body, and treating it as something to be addressed rather than scolded.

discussion.q: Before tonight, what did you privately believe anxiety was, a spiritual problem, a medical one, or a character flaw you were supposed to hide?
discussion.behind: Surface the default before defining anything. Most people in the room carry an unexamined verdict on their own worry, and it is usually a harsh one. The point is not to settle the question yet but to expose the assumption and the shame attached to it. Land it on honesty, not consensus. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Jesus does not open by rebuking the anxious. He says look at the birds. Why do you think he starts with attention rather than with a command to feel differently?
discussion.behind: Move the room off the scolding reflex. We expect Jesus to say stop it, and instead he says look. The aim is to notice that the cure begins with the eyes turned outward, not with effort turned inward. Help them feel the mercy in the method before they feel the weight of the command.

discussion.q: Bell says some anxiety is the soul reaching for the wrong refuge, and some is a body that has simply broken, and that telling them apart is the hard pastoral work. Where in your own life have you confused the two?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge of the whole study. Do not let it become a debate about whether medication is allowed. Keep it on the personal recognition that we mislabel our own worry constantly, calling sickness sin and calling sin spirituality. The honesty here protects everyone who comes after.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong form of the scolder, that Jesus does say do not be anxious and means it. What is true in that, and what does it become when it forgets the sick body?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness from the start. Jesus does give a command, and some of our worry really is the heart trusting money or control or approval. Make sure the room does not leave thinking worry is always blameless. The error is not the command. It is the command swung as a club at a person who is ill.

discussion.q: Bell confesses he has white-knuckled a morning he had no reason to fear and called it discernment. Where have you dressed up your own anxiety as something more respectable?
discussion.behind: Move from diagnosis to self-implication. You are not hunting for confession to shame anyone. You want each person, including you the leader, inside the struggle, because the gospel reaches the worried only after the worried admits the worry. Go first.

objections.objection: Anxiety is just unbelief. Jesus says do not be anxious, plainly, as a command, and if you were really trusting God you would not be falling apart. The cure is more faith, not a prescription.
objections.response: Sit with the half that is true, because Bell grants it. Jesus does command it, and some of our worry is the heart clutching the wrong thing, security or control or the good opinion of people, and that worry is addressed by trust and not by anything else. Then make the distinction with care. The same Jesus who said do not be anxious wept at a tomb and sweat as it were great drops of blood in a garden. Anxiety is not always the heart sinning. Sometimes it is the body breaking, the way a diabetic's body breaks, and you would not tell a diabetic to repent of his pancreas. To aim the command do not be anxious at a person whose adrenal system is misfiring is not faith. It is cruelty, and it drives the sick away from the very Savior who would carry them.

objections.objection: Anxiety is purely a medical condition, a matter of brain chemistry, and dragging God or the soul into it is exactly the kind of religious shaming that keeps people from getting help.
objections.response: Grant what is right, because much of it is. A body can break in ways no amount of prayer will reset, anxiety can be as physical as a fever, and the church has done real harm telling sick people to pray harder. Get the doctor. Get the help. None of that is unbelief. Then press the other edge gently. To say anxiety is only chemistry is to claim something the data cannot, that a human being is a machine and nothing more, that the dread of death and the ache of meaning are merely misfiring neurons. Some anxiety is medical and needs medicine. Some is the soul afraid of the right things in the wrong way, and that one is not healed by chemistry, because it was never only chemical. Honor the body. Do not erase the soul.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the one fear you have never said out loud to anyone, the one you carry into the dark when the house is quiet?
sessions.practice: This week, the next time the worry rises, do not fight it and do not feed it. Just name it, out loud or on paper, as plainly as you can. Then ask one honest question of it. Is this my soul reaching for a refuge that is not God, or is this my body asking for help I have refused to get. Write down what it answered, and do not judge the answer.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you know the fears we have never named, the ones we carry into the dark and tell no one. We have shamed ourselves for them, and we have let others shame us, and some of us have been sick and been told we were faithless. Forgive us, and forgive the church its cruelty. Teach us to tell the difference between the soul that needs you and the body that needs a doctor, and meet us in both. You who clothe the lilies and feed the birds, look at us. Amen.
reflection: Where have I called my own anxiety a sin when it may have been a sickness, and where have I called it a sickness when it may have been my heart trusting the wrong thing?
Have I ever let someone shame me, or shamed myself, for a worry that needed compassion and not a rebuke?
If Jesus began with look at the birds rather than with a command, what does that say about how he means to meet me in my fear?
sessions.teaching: Start where Bell starts, with a woman after a service. She told him she had prayed harder than anyone she knew and still could not breathe some mornings, and she wanted to know what she was doing wrong. She was not doing anything wrong. She was carrying something heavy, and somewhere along the way someone had told her that the carrying itself was unbelief. So we begin not with how to stop being anxious, which is where everyone wants to begin, but with the harder and more honest question. What is anxiety. Until we answer that, every cure we offer will land on the wrong wound. Take the two answers that want to silence each other, and take them at their strongest. The first says anxiety is a spiritual failure. It points to the plain words of Jesus, do not be anxious, and it concludes that worry is small faith, a refusal to trust, a sin to be repented of. And it is not entirely wrong. Jesus does say it. Some of our worry is exactly the heart clutching the wrong refuge, reaching for money or control or the good opinion of the room and panicking when the grip slips. That worry is real, and it is addressed by trust, and pretending otherwise would be its own kind of lie. The second answer says anxiety is purely medical, a chemical event in the brain, a matter of serotonin and cortisol and a body doing what bodies do, and that to bring God or the soul into it at all is the very shaming that keeps sick people from getting help. And this answer is not wrong either. A body can break. Anxiety can be as physical as a fever and as little chosen. The church has done genuine harm telling people with panic disorders to pray harder, as though the cure for a malfunctioning adrenal system were a quiet time. Now watch what happens when you refuse to let either answer win the whole field. Anxiety is not always sin, which destroys the scolder's position, because the same Jesus who said do not be anxious wept at a grave and sweat what looked like blood in a garden the night before he died. If anxiety were always unbelief, the Son of God was an unbeliever in Gethsemane, which is blasphemy. But anxiety is also not always only chemistry, which destroys the reductionist's position, because to say a human being is only a machine of neurons is a claim no microscope has ever supported, a faith statement dressed as science. The dread of death is not a misfire. It is the soul telling the truth about a world that is broken. So here is the verdict, and the leader must hold it cleanly all the way through. Anxiety is sometimes the soul afraid, sometimes the body failing, and very often both at once, tangled together so tightly that no one can fully separate them, and the pastoral work, the hard work, is to tell which without pretending you always can. Some of you in this room need to repent of a trust you have placed in something that cannot hold you. Some of you need to see a doctor and stop calling your illness a character flaw. Many of you need both, and need permission to need both. And here I have to stand inside it, because I have done the mislabeling in both directions. I have white-knuckled a morning I had no earthly reason to fear and called it discernment. I have preached peace from a pulpit on Sunday and gripped the steering wheel the whole way home. The law names the writer before the reader. Then notice how Jesus begins, because it changes everything. He does not open the most famous teaching on worry in human history with a rebuke. He does not say stop it, have more faith, what is wrong with you. He says look at the birds of the air. The cure begins with the eyes lifted, with attention turned outward and upward, toward a Father who feeds what cannot sow and clothes what cannot weave. Before he commands anything, he points. That is mercy, and it is where we will go next.

scriptureStudy.note: Therefore do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink. Notice the worry Jesus names is not exotic, it is the basics, food and body, survival. He is not addressing the worried as failures but as creatures fastened to the wrong center.

Do not be anxious about anything. Paul gives the same command, but from a prison cell, which means it is not the cheerful advice of a man whose life is easy. The command comes with a method attached, not a scolding.

Casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you. Peter assumes the anxieties are there, real, and many. He does not say you should not have them. He tells you where to put them, which is a different thing entirely.

And being in agony he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like great drops of blood. The night before the cross, the Son of God experienced something the body does under extreme distress. If anxiety were always sin, this verse could not exist.

Jesus wept. He stood at the grave of a friend he was about to raise and still wept. The grief was not a failure of faith. Some of what looks like anxiety is grief that has not finished, and grief is not a sin to be repented of.

Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me. The psalmist speaks to his own anxious soul honestly, naming the turmoil rather than denying it, then preaching hope back to himself. Scripture gives us language for the fear, not only against it.

Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. The invitation is addressed precisely to the burdened and the worn, not to people who have already mastered their peace. Anxiety is a qualification for coming, not a disqualification.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the history the church would rather forget, because we have not always handled the anxious well, and the harm has a shape worth seeing. For long stretches the Christian tradition collapsed every disturbance of the soul into the moral category of sin, so that melancholy and what we would now call clinical depression or anxiety were treated chiefly as acedia, spiritual sloth, or as a lack of trust to be confessed. There was real insight buried in that, the recognition that the soul can be sick and not only the body, but it hardened into a cruelty that left sick people doubly burdened, ill and ashamed of being ill. Set that beside the modern correction and its overcorrection. The twentieth century, with the rise of psychiatry and the discovery of how profoundly brain chemistry shapes mood, swung hard the other way, until in much of the culture anxiety became a purely medical event with no soul attached, a problem of molecules to be solved by molecules. A serious group should weigh both swings. Read the older voices honestly, where they saw that the human person is more than a chemical machine, and weigh them against the genuine medical knowledge that has rescued countless people from suffering the old framework could not touch. The discipline this whole study requires is to refuse both reductions, to hold that a person is body and soul at once, that anxiety can be sin or sickness or grief or all three, and that the cure may be repentance, or medication, or therapy, or all of them together, without the church pretending it can always tell which from the outside.

memoryVerse.text: Casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you.

sessions.title: Consider the Birds, Consider the Lilies
sessions.aim: To take seriously what Jesus actually told us to do with our worry, to look, and to see in the birds and the lilies not a denial of need but a sermon on a Father who feeds and clothes what cannot provide for itself.
sessions.summary: Jesus gives the most direct instruction in Scripture for what to do with anxiety, and it is not what we expect. He does not say analyze it, suppress it, or out-argue it. He says look at something. Look at the birds. Consider the lilies. The first question is why a Savior would answer the deepest dread of the human heart by pointing at wildlife and weeds. Bell takes the strong form of the cynic's read, that this is naive, that the birds do starve and the lilies do wither, that telling a man with no money to watch sparrows is a cruelty. He grants it weight. The birds do die. Jesus is not promising no one ever goes hungry. But the cynic misses what the argument actually is. It is not the birds never struggle. It is your Father feeds them, the lesser, and you are the greater, of more value than many sparrows. The logic runs from the small to the large, from the bird God did not die for to the child he did. Anxiety, Jesus is saying, is at bottom a failure to know whose you are. It treats God as absent when he is feeding the very sparrow on your windowsill. Then the turn. Worry adds not a single hour to your life, which means it is not even useful, only corrosive, and the kingdom Jesus tells you to seek first is not one more thing to be anxious about but the only thing that finally dissolves the anxiety. Seek first the kingdom, and the rest is your Father's problem.

keyScripture.why: Look at the birds of the air, they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them, and the argument runs from the lesser creature God provides for to the greater child he loves, naming anxiety as a failure to know whose you are.

discussion.q: Jesus answers the deepest dread of the human heart by telling us to look at birds and flowers. What is your honest first reaction to that, and what does the reaction reveal?
discussion.behind: Open on the gut response before the exegesis. Many will feel it is too simple, almost dismissive, and that instinct is exactly what Bell wants to examine. The point is to surface our resistance to so plain a remedy, because the resistance often hides our refusal to believe God actually provides.

discussion.q: Bell takes the cynic's objection seriously, that the birds do starve and the lilies do wither, so the comfort is hollow. What is true in that, and what does it miss about the actual argument Jesus is making?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The cynic is right that Jesus is not promising no one ever goes hungry. The miss is that the argument is not the birds never struggle, it is your Father feeds them and you are worth more. Help the room hear the lesser-to-greater logic, so the comfort stops sounding like denial.

discussion.q: Jesus says worry cannot add a single hour to your life. Where have you treated anxiety as if it were doing something useful, as if the worrying itself were a form of working?
discussion.behind: This is a quiet, convicting center. Many of us secretly believe our worry is responsible, that to stop worrying would be to stop caring or to drop our guard. Press on the uselessness Jesus names. The aim is to expose the lie that anxiety is a kind of labor, when it adds nothing and costs everything.

discussion.q: Bell says anxiety is, at bottom, a failure to know whose you are. Does that ring true to your experience of worry, or do you want to resist it?
discussion.behind: Let people push back honestly, because this can sound like an oversimplification and the leader must not force it. But the aim is to feel the theological diagnosis under the symptom, that much worry is an orphan's worry, the fear of a child who has forgotten he has a Father who feeds the sparrows.

discussion.q: Seek first the kingdom of God, Jesus says, and all these things will be added. How would your week be different if the kingdom, and not the rest, were the thing you sought first?
discussion.behind: Close on the reordering, with self-implication. Bell admits he seeks the rest first and tells himself he will get to the kingdom once the rest is secured, which is exactly backwards. Invite people to name what they have been seeking first, and go first yourself. The point is reordering, not resolution.

objections.objection: This is naive comfort for people with no real problems. The birds do starve. The lilies do wither. Telling a man who cannot pay rent to go watch sparrows is an insult, not a gospel.
objections.response: Bell grants the weight of this and does not win cheaply. The birds do die. Sparrows fall, and Jesus knew it, because a few verses later he says not one of them falls apart from your Father. He is not promising that no one ever goes hungry or that hardship is an illusion. Then hear what the argument actually is. It is not the birds never struggle. It is your Father feeds them, the creatures he did not make in his image, the ones he did not die for, and you are of more value than many sparrows. The logic runs from the lesser to the greater. If God attends to the bird he did not redeem, the comfort is not that you will never lack, but that you are not forgotten, not an orphan, not alone in a machine. That is not naive. That is a Father.

objections.objection: If I just stop worrying and trust God to provide like the birds, am I not being irresponsible? Should I quit planning, saving, working, and wait for food to fall from the sky?
objections.response: No, and Jesus is careful here, so we should be too. The birds do not sow or reap, but they do work, they hunt and build and feed their young from dawn to dusk. Jesus is not commending laziness. He is dismantling anxiety, which is a different thing from labor. You can work hard and plan well without lying awake rehearsing every disaster, because the working is your task and the outcome is your Father's. Anxiety is not the same as diligence. It is diligence that has lost its Father, labor that has forgotten it is not finally in charge. Seek first the kingdom, do your work as worship, and refuse the extra burden of carrying an outcome that was never yours to carry.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you truly believed the God who feeds the sparrow on your windowsill knew your name and your need, what is the worry you would lay down first?
sessions.practice: This week, do exactly what Jesus said. Once a day, stop and look at something God is keeping alive without your help, a bird, a tree, a weed pushing through the sidewalk. Watch it long enough to mean it. Then say out loud, my Father feeds that, and I am worth more than that. Write down whether saying it changed anything, even a little.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you feed the birds that do not sow and clothe the lilies that do not weave, and we have lain awake as if you did not exist, as if we were orphans running our own small kingdoms into the ground. Forgive us for the worry we mistook for responsibility. Teach us to look, really to look, until we remember whose we are. We are worth more to you than many sparrows, and you have never once forgotten a sparrow. Help us seek first your kingdom, and trust you with the rest. Amen.
reflection: What have I been treating as my problem to solve that Scripture says is my Father's to provide?
Where has my worry pretended to be useful work, when Jesus says it cannot add a single hour to my life?
If anxiety is at bottom forgetting whose I am, what would it look like to remember, today, in the next anxious moment?
sessions.teaching: Jesus gives the most direct instruction in all of Scripture for what to do with worry, and it is almost embarrassingly simple. He does not tell us to analyze our anxiety, to journal it, to argue it down, to white-knuckle our way past it. He tells us to look at something. Look at the birds of the air. Consider the lilies of the field. The question we have to sit with is why the Son of God would answer the deepest dread of the human heart by pointing at wildlife and weeds, because if we do not understand the method, we will dismiss it as a greeting card, and it is the opposite of a greeting card. Take the cynic's objection at full strength, because it is the honest one. The birds do starve. The lilies do wither and get thrown into the oven, which Jesus himself says in the very next breath. Telling a man who cannot make rent to go watch sparrows can sound like the cruelest kind of denial, the comfortable telling the desperate that their problem is a failure to appreciate nature. Grant it. Jesus is not promising that no one ever goes hungry. He is not saying hardship is an illusion or that the faithful are exempt from want. To pretend he is would be to make him a liar, because the world is full of faithful people who have known hunger. But now look at what the argument actually is, because the cynic has misread it. Jesus does not say the birds never struggle. He says your heavenly Father feeds them. The whole weight rests on that one phrase. The birds neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet they are fed, because there is a Father who attends to them. And then the hinge, the lesser-to-greater logic that runs through the entire passage. Are you not of more value than they. The God who feeds the sparrow he did not make in his image, the creature he did not redeem with his own blood, that same God is your Father, and you are worth more to him than many sparrows. The comfort is not that you will never lack. The comfort is that you are not an orphan. You are not alone in a cold machine of cause and effect. There is a Father, and he is attentive down to the smallest bird that falls, and not one of them falls apart from him. So what is anxiety, finally, in light of the birds. It is at bottom a failure to know whose you are. It is the worry of a child who has forgotten he has a Father, the dread of an orphan who believes the whole weight of his survival rests on his own two hands because no one is watching over him. And here Jesus drives in the verdict that should stop us cold. Which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life. Worry does not even work. It is not useful. It is not a form of responsibility or a kind of labor that keeps the disaster away. It adds nothing and subtracts plenty. We tell ourselves the worrying is the price of caring, that to stop would be to drop our guard, and Jesus calls the bluff. Your anxiety has never once added an hour. It has only stolen the ones you had. And I have to stand inside this, because I am the worst at it. I seek the rest first, the security and the plan and the cushion, and I tell myself I will get to the kingdom once those are nailed down, which is exactly the order Jesus forbids. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, he says, and all these things will be added to you. Not the rest first and the kingdom when there is time. The kingdom first, and the rest becomes your Father's problem, because it always was. The cure for the orphan's worry is not better self-talk. It is the recovery of a Father, the one who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies and knows your name and has never, not once, forgotten a single sparrow.

scriptureStudy.note: Look at the birds, your heavenly Father feeds them, are you not of more value than they. The argument is lesser to greater. The bird is fed though it cannot store, and you, the greater, have a Father, not merely a creator.

Which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life. Jesus names anxiety as useless, not merely sinful. It does not work, it does not lengthen life, it only corrodes the life you have.

Consider the lilies, they neither toil nor spin, yet Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. God clothes the flower more beautifully than the richest king, attending to beauty no one will see, which tells you how attentive he is.

If God so clothes the grass, which is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith. Jesus names the little faith gently, as a diagnosis, not a condemnation, and aims the comfort straight at it.

Do not be anxious, for your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. The pagans chase these things because they have no Father to know their need. The cure for anxiety is the knowledge that you are known and provided for by a Father.

Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. The reordering is the whole point. Seek the rest first and you stay anxious. Seek the kingdom first and the rest becomes the Father's concern.

Not one sparrow falls to the ground apart from your Father, and you are of more value than many sparrows. Jesus does not deny the sparrow falls. He insists the Father is present even in the falling, which is a deeper comfort than exemption.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the long Christian habit of reading the created world as a second book alongside Scripture, what the older theologians called the book of nature, because Jesus is doing something more deliberate than offering a pretty image when he points at the birds. Augustine and others spoke of creation as a text God authored to teach his creatures about himself, and the medieval tradition developed this into a whole way of seeing, in which a sparrow or a lily was not mere decoration but a sermon, a visible word about an invisible Father. Read this way, look at the birds is not Jesus changing the subject from theology to nature. It is Jesus teaching theology through nature, training the anxious eye to read providence in the ordinary. Set this beside the modern condition, in which most of us live indoors, screen-lit, and almost never look at a bird long enough to learn anything from it, and ask whether part of our anxiety is a kind of blindness, a loss of the daily evidence of a providing God that our ancestors could not avoid seeing. A serious group should weigh the danger on the other side as well, the sentimental nature-worship that turns the creation into the comfort itself rather than a pointer to the Creator, and ask how to look at the birds the way Jesus meant, through the bird to the Father, never stopping at the bird. The aim is to recover sight, the discipline of considering, which is slower and harder and more theological than glancing.
